candidates.topic: The Man Who Survived Two Atomic Bombs — Tsutomu Yamaguchi
candidates.teaser: One man was at ground zero for both Hiroshima and Nagasaki — and lived to 93. How is that even possible?
candidates.video_title: He Survived Both Atomic Bombs (True Story)
candidates.video_description: Tsutomu Yamaguchi was on a business trip in Hiroshima when the first bomb dropped. He returned home to Nagasaki just in time for the second. This is the story of history's unluckiest — or luckiest — man.
candidates.script: This man was standing 3 kilometers from the Hiroshima bomb when it detonated — burned, deafened, barely alive. So he did what anyone would do: he went home. Home was Nagasaki. Three days later, the second bomb dropped while he was describing the first one to his boss. Both blasts. Same man. Tsutomu Yamaguchi was officially recognized as a double survivor by the Japanese government in 2009. He died at 93. Was he the unluckiest human in history — or the luckiest?

candidates.topic: The Turritopsis Nutricula Colony — Coral That Votes
candidates.teaser: There's an animal on the ocean floor that makes group decisions without a single brain cell — and it outvotes us every time.
candidates.video_title: This Animal Has No Brain But Makes Decisions
candidates.video_description: Coral reefs aren't just structures — they're superorganisms capable of collective behavior. Scientists discovered that coral colonies coordinate responses to threats in ways that look disturbingly like decision-making, despite having zero neurons.
candidates.script: Coral has no brain, no eyes, no nervous system whatsoever — and yet an entire reef colony can coordinate a response to a predator within seconds. Scientists filmed thousands of individual polyps retracting in a synchronized wave, moving information across meters of reef with no neurons at all. They use chemical signals that act like a vote — majority rules, the whole colony reacts. Something with zero intelligence is making faster group decisions than most human committees. Does that say more about coral, or about us?

candidates.topic: The Philadelphia Experiment — USS Eldridge Invisibility Claim
candidates.teaser: The U.S. Navy allegedly made a warship disappear in 1943 — and what supposedly happened to the crew is far darker than invisibility.
candidates.video_title: The Navy Ship That Vanished — Then Reappeared
candidates.video_description: In October 1943, the USS Eldridge allegedly turned invisible, teleported from Philadelphia to Norfolk, and reappeared with sailors fused into the hull. The Navy denied everything. The story refuses to die.
candidates.script: In October 1943, the USS Eldridge allegedly vanished from Philadelphia Harbor — witnesses on a nearby ship watched it disappear, then reappear 400 kilometers away in Norfolk, Virginia, within minutes. When it returned, sailors were reportedly found embedded in the steel hull, others went permanently insane. The Navy erased Eldridge's logs for that date. One witness, Carl Allen, spent decades annotating a physics book with handwritten claims linking it to Einstein's unified field theory. The Navy still says none of it happened. So why are those logs missing?

candidates.topic: The Cosmic Microwave Background — You Can Hear the Big Bang
candidates.teaser: A tiny percentage of the static on an old untuned TV was literally the leftover radiation from the Big Bang — you've heard it without knowing.
candidates.video_title: You've Already Heard the Big Bang's Echo
candidates.video_description: The Cosmic Microwave Background radiation is the oldest light in the universe — 13.8 billion years old. For decades, a small portion of analog TV static was this ancient signal bleeding into everyday electronics.
candidates.script: Every time you saw static on an old television, roughly 1% of that noise was 13.8 billion years old. That fuzzy interference wasn't broken signal — it was the Cosmic Microwave Background, the literal afterglow of the Big Bang still echoing through the universe. Two Bell Lab engineers discovered it in 1965 completely by accident; they kept trying to clean pigeon droppings off their antenna, thinking the noise was interference. It wasn't. They won the Nobel Prize. The oldest thing you've ever experienced was disguised as bad TV reception.

candidates.topic: The Kowloon Walled City — Densest Human Settlement Ever
candidates.teaser: There was once a city inside a city where no government had authority — and 50,000 people built their own world completely from scratch.
candidates.video_title: The Lawless City Where 50,000 People Lived
candidates.video_description: Kowloon Walled City in Hong Kong was a 0.026 km² block of interconnected buildings housing up to 50,000 residents with no police, no sanitation authority, and no legal jurisdiction from any government. It was demolished in 1994.
candidates.script: In Hong Kong, there was a single city block where neither British nor Chinese law applied — and 50,000 people lived inside it. Kowloon Walled City was 0.026 square kilometers of interconnected high-rises so dense that the sun never reached the lower floors. Residents built their own water pipes, their own electricity grid, their own food markets. Unlicensed dentists, drug labs, and noodle factories shared the same walls. The buildings were structurally fused — one giant organism. Authorities demolished it in 1994. Would you have lived there?
